claims.text: The as-processed HEA is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution without preexisting secondary phases.
Sustained high-stress mechanical loading causes stress-induced phase decomposition in the HEA.
Stress-induced phase decomposition forms brittle intermetallic precipitates or phase-separated regions.
The stress-induced precipitates form preferentially along grain boundaries.
Sustained mechanical loading accelerates local atomic diffusion in the HEA.
Sustained mechanical loading promotes local compositional segregation.
Stress-enhanced diffusion and compositional segregation promote phase decomposition.
The resulting brittle precipitates compromise the alloy's ability to undergo plastic deformation.
The precipitates reduce fracture toughness and promote brittle fracture.
Mechanically preloaded specimens will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in K_IC relative to unloaded baseline specimens.
TEM or SEM with compositional mapping will reveal brittle intermetallic precipitates in loaded specimens that are absent in unloaded controls.
The unloaded, as-processed single-phase alloy exhibits uniformly high toughness.
The proposed behavior applies to cyclic or sustained static loading approaching or exceeding yield stress at service-relevant temperatures and environments.
Loaded and unloaded sets of otherwise identical HEA specimens provide the controlled comparison.
Variations in local composition, load profile, and temperature may affect decomposition kinetics and the magnitude of toughness reduction.
A lack of either a statistically significant toughness reduction or detectable brittle precipitate formation in loaded specimens would falsify the hypothesis.
